name: Sensation and Perception
what: This subtopic covers the distinction between sensation and perception, the three stages of perception (selection, organisation, interpretation), and the specific sensory pathways and brain regions involved in visual and gustatory perception.
why: Distinguishing sensation from perception is fundamental to understanding how raw sensory data becomes conscious experience. This underpins explanations of why two people can detect the same stimulus but perceive it differently.

items.title: I can distinguish between sensation and perception
items.what: Sensation is the process of receiving and detecting raw sensory stimuli via sensory organs and sending this information to the brain as a neural impulse. Perception is the subsequent process of selecting, organising, and interpreting that sensory information to bring it into conscious awareness.
items.why: The two processes are sequential and distinct: sensation provides the raw data, while perception gives it meaning. Conflating them leads to incorrect explanations of how we experience the world.
items.example: The eye detects light reflecting off a stop sign (sensation), and the brain then interprets the red octagonal shape as a command to stop (perception).

items.title: I can describe the three stages of perception: selection, organisation, and interpretation
items.what: Selection is the process of attending to certain stimuli and excluding others. Organisation involves regrouping the selected features into a coherent pattern. Interpretation assigns meaning to the organised information, drawing on memory, mood, and expectations.
items.why: Each stage transforms raw sensory data into a form the brain can consciously understand, and errors or influences at any stage can change what we ultimately perceive.
items.example: When seeing a smiley face drawn with simple lines: selection attends to the lines, organisation groups them into a face shape, and interpretation recognises it as expressing happiness.

items.title: I can describe the pathway of visual sensation from the eye to the brain
items.what: Visual sensation begins when light enters the eye through the pupil and is focused by the lens onto the retina. Sensory receptors in the retina convert the light energy into a neural impulse, which is sent to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe for perceptual processing.
items.why: Understanding this pathway clarifies where in the process biological abnormalities (such as myopia or colour blindness) can alter what we see.
items.example: When a person looks at a green apple, light from the apple travels through the lens, hits the retina, is converted to a neural signal, and is processed in the occipital lobe.

items.title: I can describe the pathway of gustatory sensation from the tongue to the brain
items.what: Gustatory sensation begins when saliva breaks food into tastants, which are detected by gustatory receptors within taste buds on the tongue and around the mouth. The signal is converted to a neural impulse and sent to the primary gustatory cortex in the parietal lobe.
items.why: Knowing the gustatory pathway explains how factors like reduced saliva production with age or fewer taste buds affect the intensity of flavour we perceive.
items.example: When eating a piece of dark chocolate, the bitter tastants are detected by gustatory receptors on the tongue and the neural signal travels to the parietal lobe for processing.

items.title: I can name the five basic flavours detected by the gustatory system
items.what: The five basic flavours are sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami (savoury). These are the fundamental categories of taste that gustatory receptors are sensitive to, and complex flavour experiences are built from combinations of these.
items.why: Understanding the five basic flavours clarifies why removing one sensory input (such as smell) can reduce the richness of flavour perception even though the tastants themselves are unchanged.
items.example: Coffee is primarily bitter (one of the five basic flavours), which is why children with more taste buds tend to find it unpleasant, while adults with fewer taste buds may find it more tolerable.

items.title: I can explain how other senses contribute to gustatory perception
items.what: Gustatory perception is not limited to taste alone; the senses of smell, vision, and touch (texture) all contribute. The gustatory cortex integrates information from the olfactory cortex (smell) and the somatosensory cortex (texture) to form a complete perception of flavour.
items.why: This integration explains everyday experiences such as food tasting blander when you have a blocked nose, and why the colour or texture of food can change how its flavour is perceived.
items.example: When eating a strawberry, the sweet taste is combined with the fruity smell and soft texture to produce the full perception of strawberry flavour; blocking the nose reduces this richness.
